Live DOM vs Always GPU
ICE · widgetlab-desktop · stress rig · 2026-09-09

Live DOM vs Always GPU

Many DOM cards, every one of them running a looping CSS animation, measured under the two standard surface behaviours the engine ships: live DOM at rest, the default, against always through the GPU copy. Fresh Electron process per cell, arms interleaved, medians of two rounds on a loaded host.

arm dom · ice:surface.domAtRest

Live DOM at rest

Chromium paints and composites every card. The ground draws chrome and field and otherwise sleeps. The GPU takes a card only while it is grabbed.

The answer

The two policies do not differ by a factor. They differ by which resource runs out first.

With nothing animating, both arms are idle-zero and cost the same: no submit, no copy, a main thread at rest. The moment cards animate at rest, the always-GPU arm turns every paint event into a whole-card copy, and this host will do about – of those a second no matter how many cards ask. Below that ceiling the arm holds 120 fps; above it the frame rate is the ceiling divided by the card count, which is – fps at 96 cards, – at 192 and – at 384. Lowering the demand bucket helps only while the bucket times the card count is under the ceiling.

The live-DOM arm rides Chromium's compositor for transform and opacity animations, so its main thread stays idle and it holds 120 fps at every board size on that kind of animation. It is not free: paint-driven animation, where a width or a colour changes every frame, is a main-thread paint of every card, and it falls to – fps at 192 cards and – at 384. It also pays two things the copy arm never does: a stall on the first frame of a pan that grows with the card count, reaching – ms at 384 cards, and a GPU-process footprint that grows with every animated layer, reaching – MB after the camera phases where the copy arm sits at – MB.

For the product this settles the default the record already ratified. A board of a few dozen animating cards is fine on either arm. Past about forty animators the copy arm's frame rate is arithmetic, and past a hundred it is a slideshow, while the live-DOM arm keeps its frame rate and pays in memory and one stall per pan. The right unit of decision is the widget, not the board: a card that animates at rest belongs on the live DOM, and a card that is still at rest can take the copy for its true z and effects at no running cost.

The rig

One process per cell, the same board on both arms

The rig is a page of the desktop app, apps/widgetlab-desktop/stress.html, mounted on the composited profile with the ground as compositor and the app-owned WebGPU device. It defines two widget types with one component: stress-dom takes the engine's default behaviour and stress-gpu declares alwaysGpu. The board is a grid of 150 by 100 unit cards, zoomed to fit the 1280 by 808 viewport so every card is visible, because a culled card folds to paused demand and would measure nothing. Each step of the ladder doubles the board: 24, 48, 96, 192, 384 cards.

Every card carries the same content: a title, two lines of text, a rotating ring and a fading dot on their own will-change layers, and a bar whose width animates beside a block whose colour cycles. One attribute on the document switches which pair runs, so the switch itself costs the measurement nothing. The two pairs are different questions for a live-DOM arm. Transform and opacity ride Chromium's compositor thread with no main-thread paint. Width and colour force layout and paint of the card every frame. The copy arm cannot tell them apart: inside the source canvas every animation frame is a paint event.

Each phase is a four-second window after a discarded settle. The page counts rAF frames and their intervals, the time spent inside rAF callbacks on the main thread, long tasks, and the ground's own instruments: submits, redraws, copies, paint marks, the clamp's parked and deferred sets, page layers. The driver adds per-process CPU from Electron's own accounting, calibrated against a deliberately busy main thread, and physical footprints from vmmap. A fresh Electron process runs each cell, the order of cells is reversed on the second round, and every result is the median of the rounds with the raw windows kept in the JSON.

Two witnesses back the counters. The spinner and the bar are captured several times a few hundred milliseconds apart and the differing pixels counted, on the first and the last card, so a copy that lands from a stale paint record cannot pass as motion. On the copy arm, the first card's slot in the page array is also read back and hashed at the same cadence, which says whether the copy itself brings new texels.

Frames

Where each arm stops keeping up

Compositor-driven animation is the live-DOM arm's best case and the copy arm's worst. Chromium animates transform and opacity off the main thread, so the live-DOM arm holds the panel's 120 Hz at every size. The copy arm cannot use the compositor: every animation frame is a paint event, every paint event a whole-card copy, and the copies are what set its frame rate.

Paint-driven animation narrows the gap. Both arms now pay a main-thread paint per card per frame. The live-DOM arm keeps 120 fps to 96 cards and then falls as the main thread saturates. The copy arm pays the same paint and then the copy on top, so it falls first and further.

The copy ceiling

About – whole-card copies a second, whatever the card count

The ceiling is a rate, not a bandwidth. From 96 to 384 cards the copies per second stay on a plateau while the slot shrinks from 300 by 200 texels to 150 by 100, so bytes are not what saturates. Each copy is one rasterisation of the element's paint record inside the GPU process, and that process's CPU sits on the same plateau across the same range. The main thread is not busy during this: its rAF time is mostly waiting on the copy call.

The demand bucket is a lever only below the ceiling. At 96 cards a bucket of 15 brings the ask under the plateau and the frame rate back to 120. At 192 and 384 even a bucket of 15 asks for more copies than the host can make, so the bucket changes nothing.

The main thread

What one animating card costs the whole board

On the copy arm a single spinner wakes a full-board frame build. With one card animating and every other card still, the copy arm's rAF time per frame grows with the card count, because each copy touches the residency, which wakes the frame builder, which resolves every on-screen card and encodes a full pass. The live-DOM arm's engine loop stays at its idle floor: the animation never reaches it.

With every card animating the copy arm's rAF time is the copy loop itself. At 384 cards the flush spends over a hundred milliseconds inside one rAF callback, and the platform reports it as a long task on every frame.

Pan and zoom

The live-DOM arm's stall, and the copy arm's band crossing

The live-DOM arm pays one long frame when a pan starts, and it scales with the card count. About 1.6 ms per card: – ms at 96, – at 192, – at 384. The profile below puts it in the DOM clip writer: on the pan's first frames the clip key of every live-DOM card changes, so its 720-ray clip polygon is marched again and written as a new clip-path, and Chromium then re-styles and repaints every card behind it. The same writer runs under the copy arm and recomputes nothing. The rig sampled the resolved-geometry fields the key reads on the pan's first frames and none of them moved; the other thing the key carries is the card's content rect, which the builder takes from the host's measured size where one exists, and only live-DOM hosts are measured. So the key moves once per live-DOM card when its measurement lands or shifts at the pan's start, and never on the copy arm, whose hosts are unmeasured by design. The fix belongs to the writer: key the clip off the durable size, or ignore a sub-pixel change.

A band crossing re-copies every visible card on the copy arm. The zoom leaves the held band and comes back, and each crossing is a burst of one copy per card in one flush. The live-DOM arm re-rasters at the new scale inside Chromium and shows it as a shorter dip.

Where the time goes

The main thread, sampled

Memory

The copy arm's memory is flat. The live-DOM arm's grows with every animated layer.

While the board animates, the copy arm's GPU process sits near – MB at every size. The whole board lives in one or two 16 MB page layers, and a copy writes into a slot that already exists. The live-DOM arm's footprint grows with the animated layers instead: every ring and every dot is a composited layer with its own tiles, two per card, from – MB at 24 cards to – MB at 384.

The camera phases add memory on both arms, for different reasons. On the copy arm a band crossing allocates a second band's slots, and the residency keeps them within its 256 MB budget, so the arm lands between – and – MB whatever the board. On the live-DOM arm the zoom leaves Chromium holding tiles for every animated layer at a second scale, and at 384 cards the GPU process reaches – MB. That memory is Chromium's to shed under pressure, and the lever is the number of will-change layers a widget declares.

The witnesses

Do the pixels move

What it means

Choose per widget, not per board

  • Keep domAtRest as the default. Anything that animates at rest, takes text, or scrolls stays on the live DOM. The stress board is the case the record's Q5 ruling was made for, and the numbers agree with it.
  • Use alwaysGpu for cards that are still at rest. Charts, pictures, cards that change only on data. They copy once, idle-zero holds, and they gain true z and WGSL effects. A still card costs nothing on either arm; only a moving one pays the copy.
  • Budget animators, not cards. On this host the copy arm has about – copies a second to spend. At 120 Hz that is about twenty cards animating at full rate; at 60, forty; at a bucket of 15, about a hundred and fifty. Beyond that the frame rate is arithmetic.
  • Two things to fix on the live-DOM arm, both in the engine's own code. The first-frame stall of a pan grows linearly with the card count and reaches – ms at 384 cards; the profile names it. And a board of hundreds of animating cards leaves Chromium holding well over a gigabyte in the GPU process after a zoom; that is Chromium's tile memory for the animated layers, and the lever is the number of will-change layers a widget declares.
  • One fidelity item on the copy arm, found by the witness that disagreed. Under band raster a DOM card's host box is band space, so a widget laid out in pixels reflows and clips at every band but 1: at band 0.5 the stress card loses its bar and colour block off the right edge and shows its title at twice the relative size. The live-DOM arm never reflows. Widgets that take the copy need to size in the box's own units, or the profile needs to keep the box at world size and scale the content by the band.
After this report

The drag now promotes the board, as stills

Ruled the same day from these numbers: dragging a DOM card must not leave the carried card under its resting neighbours, and since the copy arm is the slower one, the cards promoted for a gesture are rendered once and held. Two engine changes landed on ICE main with the rig extended to prove them on the live composited app.

  • The gesture set. A grab on any DOM card now promotes every DOM card of the default behaviour in the same step, each as a still: one picture at promotion, paused for the gesture, the whole set demoted one settle window after the last release with every card's own cadence restored. DomRender gained the rule that makes a still possible, a paused card takes its first picture when the world names its destination, then parks.
  • Held cards paint last. The rig's overlap witness caught a second defect on both arms: the ground painted in sibling order and a grab raised nothing, so a carried card slid under any later sibling it crossed. The frame builder now draws held cards after the rest, which is the lifted plane's rule on the ground.

Measured on the desktop app at 120 Hz with the rig's new drag phase: at 24 cards the grab promotes all 24 as stills in one step with one plate frame and a 50 ms pickup, the carry runs at 118 fps on 24 copies in total, and the set is back on the live DOM 600 ms after the release with no further copies. At 96 cards the pickup is 167 ms, about 1.7 ms per card for the reparent and the first copy, the carry 112 fps on 96 copies. The overlap pixel reads the carried card on both arms; before the builder fix it read the card under it on both.

After this report · the copy's cost, named

Why a copy costs half a millisecond whatever its size

Asked the same day: why does the always-GPU arm fall so far behind live DOM, and what is the actual bottleneck? Three witnesses answer it, and they agree. Chromium's own source for this build (150.0.7871.114), a Chrome trace of the composited app at 24 and 192 cards, and a micro-benchmark that copies elements with no engine in the loop at all.

The pipeline, per call. Every copyElementImageToTexture takes the element's cached paint record, creates a brand-new GPU resource provider for it, rasterises the record into that fresh surface through the out-of-process raster channel, wraps the surface for Dawn, blits it into the destination with CopyTextureForBrowser, and destroys the surface. Nothing is kept between calls. The trace shows what that means on the GPU process's main thread, which runs all of it single-file:

Stage of one copy (GPU process main thread, traced at 192 cards)ms per copysharewhat it is
Raster: begin, replay the record, end (Graphite recording + a Metal submit)0.2956 %4 render passes per card (the card's three translucent groups each open one) and one command-buffer commit per copy; the draw calls inside are 0.03 ms of it
Shared image create + destroy0.0612 %one IOSurface-backed surface per copy, the card's size, thrown away after the blit
WebGPU decoder: wrap the surface, CopyTextureForBrowser, unwrap0.0816 %two Dawn command batches per copy
Scheduling and flushes0.0916 %8 GPU-channel requests and 4 command-buffer flushes per copy
Total on that one thread0.52100 %the same at 24 cards (0.54) and at 192 (0.52); 97 % busy at 192

At 24 cards that thread is 58 % busy and the renderer never waits. At 192 it is saturated, and the renderer's main thread spends 43 % of every frame inside GpuChannel::WaitForGetOffsetInRange, blocked by command-buffer flow control until the GPU process catches up. That wait is what the sampled profile in the section above reported as time "inside" the copy call. The renderer's own work per copy is small: 0.05 ms to serialise the paint record onto the raster channel and 0.10 ms of Dawn wire flushes.

Measured without the engine. The micro-benchmark puts N cards under one layoutsubtree canvas and copies them into a page array with nothing else running. Its ceiling is the same one the app hit, so DomRender adds nothing to the problem: the engine's 0.03 to 0.05 ms of main-thread bookkeeping per copy is noise against Chromium's 0.5 ms of GPU-process time.

A 44× range of texels per copy moves the cost by 14 %. Simpler content moves it by 10 %. The destination does not move it. The count of cards does not move it. It is a fixed cost per call.

The lever is the number of calls, and it was measured. A wrapper element that is the canvas's immediate child can hold many cards, and one call copies all of them. Sweeping how many cards share a call gives the cost's two parts directly: about 0.58 ms per call plus about 0.05 ms per card of content.

Eight times the cards per second, and at that point the display, not the GPU process, is the limit. Live DOM never enters this pipeline at all: a compositor-driven animation repaints nothing, and a paint-driven one rasterises only the invalidated tiles, in batches, on the compositor's raster worker threads, into surfaces that persist from frame to frame. That is the whole difference between the two arms. One is a per-element, allocate-every-time, single-threaded copy; the other is a batched, persistent, parallel raster.

Asked next: how to optimise it, and whether a newer Chromium already has. The same page ran on three runtimes back to back. Electron 44 with Chromium 152 copies at the same per-call cost as 150; the Electron 45 alpha with Chromium 155 is 20 to 30 percent slower per call and a 24-card board no longer holds 120 fps on it. Chromium's main branch still builds a fresh resource provider for every call; what it adds is API, a detached ElementImage and a draw with a source rectangle and a size, not a cache. Two runtime switches were tried and both lose: the unaccelerated element path moves 0.45 ms per copy onto the main thread and lowers the ceiling to 2,000 calls a second, and the Ganesh backend copies at 2,500 a second and drops a 24-card board to 41 fps.

The budget changes no runtime and no design: at most K copies a frame, fairly rotated over the dirty cards, so the whole app keeps the display's rate at any board size and only the promoted cards' cadence degrades. Today the same boards run everything, pans and the lifted card included, at 15 and 7 fps. The 2D route is the structural lever that keeps the hit-test: a draw into the source canvas puts the cached record straight into the canvas's own recording, so N dirty cards raster as one recording with one submit, and one copy of the canvas lands them in the page array. Its limit is GPU time from the translucent groups in the card, not the GPU process's thread, which is why flat content runs three times faster on it at the same CPU. It reopens an earlier decision that deleted a 2D atlas for its memory; that atlas was sized to the board, this one to the viewport.

Built and measured in the engine. Both levers now exist behind one option on the compose host, off by default: a copy budget with an adaptive controller, and the batched 2D route with the element copy as its fallback. The same rig ran four variants alone, one round each, on the day's host (whose base was slower than the sweep above: 48, 12 and 6 fps at 96, 192 and 384 cards).

The budget is the frame-rate lever and the batch is the throughput lever, and together they give the budget's frame rate at three times the cadence. Past 192 cards neither reaches the display's rate, because the main thread is then busy with its own per-frame paint of every animating host inside the source canvas, a cost live DOM never pays. The batched route's own limit is the hardware: a trace shows the display compositor's swap waiting for Dawn's commands to be scheduled, three render passes per card draw for the card's translucent groups. And the pickup does not move under either lever. A profile of that frame puts 153 of its 178 ms in the DOM clip writer, which marches 720 rays of the card program's distance field per promoted host and caches by element, so 96 cards sharing one clip key compute the same polygon 96 times. A memo keyed by the clip key is the fix, and it is recorded, not landed.

What that means for the engine. The wrapper is not a free change. A card's host is laid out at its on-screen position because that host is the card's hit-test, focus and caret truth, and a wrapper copies its children where they are laid out, so a page-shaped wrapper would need its hosts at slot positions and lose the hit-test, while a viewport-shaped wrapper keeps the hosts where they are and copies the board as one screen-space picture, in which DOM cards are already composited over each other and the ground can only reorder what it copies separately. That trade, and where it pays (the gesture set already pays one copy per card at pickup, and a board of 96 cards would pay 2 calls instead of 96), is the design question this measurement opens. It is recorded, not decided.

Reproduce

Run it again

cd infinite-canvas-engine/apps/widgetlab-desktop
TMPDIR=/tmp STRESS_ARMS=dom,gpu STRESS_N=24,48,96,192,384 STRESS_ROUNDS=2 STRESS_WINDOW_MS=4000 \
  pnpm run stress          # builds, then runs scripts/stress.mjs; JSON + screenshots in screenshots/stress/

# the profile mode: an unminified bundle so function names survive
pnpm exec vite build --minify false --outDir dist-profile
TMPDIR=/tmp STRESS_PROFILE=1 STRESS_DIST=dist-profile STRESS_N=96,192,384 STRESS_ROUNDS=1 \
  node scripts/stress.mjs

# the copy's cost: a Chrome trace of the composited app, and the no-engine micro-benchmark
TMPDIR=/tmp TRACE_N=192 pnpm run hic:trace     # screenshots/hic-trace/trace-gpu-192.json (≈240 MB)
TMPDIR=/tmp pnpm run hic:micro                  # screenshots/hic-micro/micro-.json
